theme: Doctrinal Pause: Covenant Theology, A Framework
summary: The biblical covenants as the structure of redemptive history (progressive covenantalism)
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 15:1-21 again, then Jeremiah 31:31-34 and Hebrews 8:6-13. These three passages span the Bible’s covenantal arc: the Abrahamic covenant, the promise of the new covenant, and the New Testament’s announcement that the new covenant has come in Christ. Read them with the question in mind: what is a covenant, and why is it the structure of God’s relationship with his people?
settingTheScene: Yesterday you read the formal cutting of the Abrahamic Covenant, God alone walking between the pieces, binding himself to keep what he had promised. Today we pause to think more carefully about what covenants are and how they shape the entire Bible. Covenant is not a technical theological term invented by scholars. It is the Bible’s own primary category for describing how God relates to his people. From Noah to Abraham to Moses to David to the new covenant in Christ, God always relates to his people through covenant. Understanding this category is essential for reading the Bible well.
observation: Genesis 15 shows the basic pattern of a covenant: a sovereign initiates, makes promises, and seals them with an oath ceremony.
The Hebrew word berith (“covenant”) first appears with Noah (Genesis 6:18), then runs through Abraham, Moses, David, and the prophets.
Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises a “new covenant” that will be different from the one God made when he brought Israel out of Egypt.
The new covenant features: law written on hearts, all knowing the LORD, sins forgiven and remembered no more.
Hebrews 8 explicitly identifies Christ as the mediator of this new covenant.
Christ’s institution of the Lord’s Supper uses the language of Jeremiah 31: “this is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20).
Every major covenant has a sign: rainbow (Noahic), circumcision (Abrahamic), Sabbath (Mosaic), throne (Davidic), the Lord’s Supper (New).
The covenants build on one another, each new covenant fulfills what the previous covenants promised.
doctrinalFocus:
A covenant, in the biblical sense, is a sworn relationship of personal commitment between God and his people. It is more than a contract, which is a transaction between equals for limited purposes. A covenant is a personal bond, sealed with promises and signs, that creates a relationship of mutual belonging. God says, in essence: I will be your God, and you will be my people.

The Bible’s story is structured around a series of covenants. Each one builds on the others, fulfilling earlier promises while opening new dimensions. Understanding this structure is essential for reading Scripture well.

The first covenant in Scripture is the covenant with Noah (Genesis 9). It is universal, made with all humanity and all creation, and its purpose is preservation. God commits to maintain the natural order so that the larger story of redemption can unfold. The sign is the rainbow. This covenant is still in effect today.

The second is the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12, 15, 17). It narrows from all humanity to one family, but with a promise that will eventually re-expand to bless all the families of the earth. Three things are promised: land, offspring, and universal blessing. The sign is circumcision. As you have just seen in Genesis 15, this covenant is unconditional, God alone walks between the pieces.

The third is the covenant with Moses at Sinai (Exodus 19-24). This is a covenant with the nation of Israel, organizing them as God’s people under his law. Unlike the Abrahamic Covenant, this one has conditions, blessings for obedience, curses for disobedience. The sign is the Sabbath. The Mosaic Covenant does not replace the Abrahamic; it serves it, providing the structure by which Abraham’s offspring would live as God’s holy people in the land of promise.

The fourth is the covenant with David (2 Samuel 7). God promises David an everlasting throne. From his line will come a king whose kingdom will never end. The sign is the Davidic dynasty itself. This narrows further still, from a nation to a family within that nation, from a family to a king who will rule forever.

The fifth and final is the new covenant, promised in Jeremiah 31 and ratified in Christ. This is not merely another covenant; it is the fulfillment of all the others. Jeremiah describes it: God’s law written on hearts (rather than tablets of stone), every member knowing the LORD personally (rather than learning from others), and sins forgiven definitively. The new covenant accomplishes what the Mosaic Covenant could not, it makes the relationship between God and his people internal, personal, and permanent.

Christians have debated for centuries how exactly the covenants relate to one another. Some traditions emphasize discontinuity, the new covenant is largely replacing the old. Other traditions emphasize continuity, the new covenant fulfills and extends the old. The framework this plan follows, sometimes called progressive covenantalism, sees the covenants as a unified, unfolding story. Each builds on the previous. Each is fulfilled in Christ. The Old Testament is not a different religion from the New Testament; it is the same story moving toward the same goal.

Several things follow from this. First, God always relates to his people through covenant. He does not deal with humanity merely as Creator or Lawgiver or Judge, but as covenant Lord, one who has bound himself to a people. Second, covenant is the structure of grace. Every covenant is initiated by God, not earned by humans. Even the conditional Mosaic Covenant comes only after God has already redeemed Israel from Egypt. Grace comes first; obligation responds. Third, the covenants are interconnected. The Abrahamic promise that all nations would be blessed finds its fulfillment in the new covenant, where Gentiles are grafted in. The Davidic promise of an everlasting king finds its fulfillment in Christ, whose throne is eternal. Fourth, Christ is the center. Every covenant points toward him. He is the offspring of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), the prophet greater than Moses (Hebrews 3:1-6), the Son of David, and the mediator of the new covenant.
interpretation:
The three passages you read together tell the covenantal story of the Bible in three frames. Genesis 15 shows the unconditional commitment of God to Abram. Jeremiah 31 promises a new covenant that will accomplish what the Mosaic Covenant could not. Hebrews 8 declares that Christ is the mediator of this new covenant.

Look at Jeremiah 31:31 carefully. “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke.” The Mosaic Covenant was broken. Despite all of God’s faithfulness, Israel could not be faithful in return. The law written on tablets of stone did not transform stone hearts. A new covenant was needed, one that would do something the old could not do.

And then Jeremiah lists the features of this new covenant. Three things stand out. First, the law will be written on hearts. The same God who etched the Ten Commandments on tablets at Sinai will now etch his law on the hearts of his people. Internal, not external. Second, all will know the LORD, from the least to the greatest. No more need for one Israelite to teach another to know the LORD; the relationship will be personal and universal. Third, sins will be forgiven and remembered no more. The sacrificial system of the Mosaic Covenant had to be repeated endlessly because the sins kept piling up. The new covenant deals with sin definitively.

Hebrews 8 then identifies the mediator of this new covenant: Christ. By his death, the new covenant has been ratified. By his Spirit, the law is being written on his people’s hearts. By his blood, sins are forgiven and remembered no more. The promise of Jeremiah 31 has been fulfilled. The covenant cut with Abram, sealed with God alone walking through the pieces, finds its ultimate fulfillment when Christ is torn on the cross, the divine party of the covenant bearing the curse so that the blessing of Abraham could come to all nations.

This is what it means to read the Bible covenantally. You do not see disconnected stories or random commandments. You see one God, one people, and one covenant promise unfolding in stages, each stage building on the last, all of them finding their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).
connection: Today’s doctrinal pause names what has been happening throughout your reading. God has been relating to his people through covenants from the beginning. Noah, Abraham, and the others you have read about are all participants in this single unfolding story. When you read the rest of the Old Testament, you will see Moses, David, and the prophets, each adding new dimensions to the covenantal story. And when you reach the New Testament, you will see Christ as the climax: the offspring of Abraham, the prophet like Moses, the Son of David, the mediator of the new covenant. The whole Bible is one story, and covenant is its spine.
application:
If you are a Christian, you are a covenant person. You are not relating to God merely as a generic worshiper or a religious seeker. You are bound to him by the new covenant in Christ’s blood. Three implications follow.

First, your relationship with God is secure. Like Abram’s covenant, the new covenant rests on God’s commitment, not yours. The Father has bound himself to you in Christ. The Spirit has been given as the seal. You cannot break a covenant whose maintenance depends on God. Your assurance is grounded here.

Second, your relationship with God is communal. Covenants always create peoples, not just individuals. You are part of the church, the people of the new covenant. The Lord’s Supper you share with other believers is the sign of this covenant. Do not try to live the Christian life alone. The covenant binds you to one another, not just to God.

Third, your relationship with God is transformational. The new covenant promised hearts changed, sins forgiven, and an intimate knowledge of the LORD. These are not future promises; they are present realities for everyone in Christ. The Spirit is writing God’s law on your heart even now. Your sins are forgiven and remembered no more. You know the LORD, however dimly, because he has revealed himself to you. Live in light of this. You are not who you were. You are a new-covenant person, in Christ, by grace.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he binds himself to his people by promise, and ask him to make that real to you.
Thank Jesus as the mediator of the new covenant.
Ask him to help you live out of that security, together with his people.
